newsitem.title: USA: Stocks, bonds and dollar dogged by rumors and worries.
newsitem.headline: Stocks, bonds and dollar dogged by rumors and worries.

text.p: Stocks, bonds and the dollar plunged Wednesday as investors faced a wall of worries about the strength of U.S. financial markets.

A flurry of unsubstantiated rumours and speculation that Japanese investors were no longer willing to be a big buyers of U.S. Treasury bonds also unleashed across-the-board selling, wiping off more than 100 points from the Dow Jones industrial average for the second time in less than a week.
In early afternoon, the world's most closely watched stock market index was off 113.41 points at 6,359.84.

In the U.S. Treasuries market, the benchmark 30-year bond was off 1-1/4 points, or $12.50 per $1,000 face value, boosting its yield, which moves in the opposite direction, to 6.59 percent from 6.49 percent Tuesday.
The dollar was also under the gun, dropping to 1.5365 German marks from 1.5530 marks on Tuesday and sank to 112.80 Japanese yen from 113.40 yen.

Gold, a safe haven in times of uncertainty, was flat as the market again failed to benefit from the stock market jitters. February gold was unchanged at $370.50 an ounce on New York's Commodity Exchange.

Analysts said the stock market was dogged by rumours at a time when it had rebounded after stiff selling last Friday on cautionary comments by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan about "irrational exuberance" in financial markets.

The Fed chief's comments, which fuelled worries that the central bank might step in to cool things off by raising interest rates, sparked a headlong drop of 145 points in the Dow before it rallied to end with a loss of 55 points.
This time, the market was rattled by worries that Japanese investors might cut their holdings of U.S. stocks and bonds.

Also rattling stocks, which on Monday bounced back nicely from Friday's sell-off, were rumours that International Business Machines Corp. -- a pacesetter among blue-chip stocks -- was about to issue a profit warning.
An IBM spokesman declined to comment and said the company had no plans to issue a press release Wednesday. IBM lost $4 to $154.
Goldman, Sachs & Co., addressing another rumour, said its market strategist Abby Joseph Cohen, long bullish on U.S. stocks, had not made any new comments.

"The tone is very nervous because we've had a huge runup in such a short period of time," said one trader, who noted that big institutional investors had stepped to the sidelines and there did not seem to be any general panic.
Traders said a new focus in the bond market was whether Japan would continue to support the U.S. Treasury market.
John Breazeale, president of Weiss Money Management Inc. in Palm Beach Gardens, Fla., said the heavy ownership of U.S. debt by foreigners has been an "obvious problem" for some time.
He said that foreigners own almost $1 trillion out of a total of $5.1 trillion outstanding.

There were also concerns about a column in the Wall Street Journal that questioned whether Japanese institutions were losing their appetite for U.S. Treasuries, which sent the bond market down sharply.

In an interview on Reuters Financial Television, Goldman Sachs International Vice Chairman Robert Hormats said he expected institutional investors in Japan could begin to trim the pace of their investment in U.S. Treasuries, but said he did not expect a "wholesale pullback" in demand.
Earlier, analysts cited similar comments by Hormats that appeared in the newspaper as pressing Treasuries in overnight trading outside the United States.
The bond market ignored good news from the inflation front.

The Labour Department said the Producer Price Index rose 0.4 percent last month, matching the 0.4 percent rise in October. But the core rate, which excludes food and energy, rose by only 0.1 percent. Economists had expected a 0.2 percent rise.
"The numbers confirm a continuation of relatively low inflation in the underlying economy," said Joseph Battipaglia, chief investment officer at Gruntal & Co.
